89:## The curator's role and decisions
90-
91-The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.
92-
93-The revival resolves the contradictions that the team left, by the evidence in the repository: the specification, the papers, the library and the code. The curator does not redesign the language, and decides a contradiction that the evidence leaves open, by the designers' intent. The curator's words show what the curator decided. They are not the ground of the design.
94-
95-Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.
96-
97-Weigh a team text by its provenance: who wrote it, in which role, such as a core designer or an outside contributor of the open-source years, and whether the team reviewed it or its author called it provisional. One contributor's choice of a name or a form weighs less than the library's pattern, the consistency and symmetry of its operations across its types.
98-
99-A decision is consequential if it:
100-

POSITIONS.md:100
- P-166 **`ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects, and the specification's list of reference objects stops naming arbitrary-precision numbers.** The library declares `value object BigNum extends ZZ` (`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:565`, `.fsi:223`), so every `ZZ` value is a value object, and `QQ`'s object `Ratio` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:648`) is a `value object` too. By the specification's rule two value objects of one type are strictly equivalent when their fields are, so two `ZZ` values built apart are `SEQV` when their integers are equal, `SEQV` converting each into its bits and comparing those, and two equal rationals built apart are `SEQV` in the same way. The specification's list in `Specification/basic/objects.tex` ("Reference objects include arbitrary-precision numbers") is revised to name them among the value objects, in the revision form (P-96) with one Appendix I entry. Why: the library's `value` declaration is the deliberate word, and where it is, the curator's rule brings the specification's example in line with the code. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4, point 11, which found the split.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:76
- P-169 **The runtime's own 13 native bindings, the arrays' store, threads with `abort` and the task trace, name compiled helpers that walk's loader answers with walk's own operations, P-167's device, in two compiled shapes.** Each keeps P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the compiled path runs; walk's loader answers the name with walk's glue, so walk keeps its `AtomicArray` store and its `spawn`, and for these names P-58's walk half bends, as for P-167's two. The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are on a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85; F-333). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is (F-335); `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals' 24 bindings, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, leave the library with those two types (P-174), so no carrier is designed for them; `IntLiteral`'s other 8, its conversions and comparisons, are Fortress text over its `asZZ` (F-331). A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run. Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. Detail: `reviews/natives-device-2026-11-07.md`, sections 3.1 to 3.4; the store's shape: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q2.
